## InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., *Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback*)

**Objective (Eq. 2, p. 9):**

$$
\text{objective}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim D_{\pi_\phi^{RL}}}\Big[r_\theta(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\phi^{RL}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{SFT}(y\mid x)}\Big]+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D_{\text{pretrain}}}\big[\log\pi_\phi^{RL}(x)\big]
$$

- $\pi_\phi^{RL}$ is the policy being trained. $\pi^{SFT}$ is the supervised model, and $D_{\text{pretrain}}$ is the pretraining distribution (p. 9).
- $\beta$ sets the strength of the KL penalty and $\gamma$ the strength of the pretraining gradients. With $\gamma = 0$ the model is called "PPO"; with $\gamma > 0$ it is "PPO-ptx", which is what the paper calls InstructGPT (p. 9).
- The objective is optimised with PPO in a bandit setting. A random prompt is shown, the reward model scores the response, and the episode ends. The KL penalty is applied per token against the SFT model "to mitigate over-optimization of the reward model" (p. 9).
- They used $\beta = 0.02$ and $\gamma = 27.8$ (p. 42).
- The $\gamma$ term was added to fix performance drops on public NLP datasets (p. 9). Raising the KL coefficient alone does not fix those drops, even at $\beta = 2.0$, which is 100× the default (pp. 15, 53). Setting $\beta$ to 0 or to 2 both gave poor human ratings (p. 56).

## DPO (Rafailov et al., *Direct Preference Optimization*)

**Starting RL objective (Eq. 3, pp. 3–4):**

$$
\max_{\pi_\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim D,\,y\sim\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}\big[r_\phi(x,y)\big]-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{KL}\big[\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\big]
$$

- $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the initial SFT model. The constraint keeps the policy close to the data on which the reward model is accurate, keeps generations diverse and prevents collapse onto a single high-reward answer (p. 4).
- The paper notes that standard practice optimises this with PPO, using the reward $r_\phi - \beta(\log\pi_\theta - \log\pi_{\text{ref}})$ (p. 4).

**How DPO turns this into a supervised loss:**
1. The optimal policy has a closed form: $\pi_r(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\!\big(\tfrac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\big)$ (Eq. 4, p. 4).
2. Rearranging gives the reward in terms of the policy: $r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}+\beta\log Z(x)$ (Eq. 5, p. 4).
3. Substituting this into the Bradley–Terry preference model cancels $Z(x)$, because only differences between rewards matter (p. 4). This gives the loss (Eq. 7, p. 4):

$$
\mathcal{L}_{DPO}=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim D}\Big[\log\sigma\Big(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\Big)\Big]
$$

## How they differ

| | InstructGPT | DPO |
|---|---|---|
| KL-regularised core | Expected RM reward minus $\beta\cdot$ log-ratio to $\pi^{SFT}$ (p. 9) | The same form, written as an explicit $\mathbb{D}_{KL}$ to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ (pp. 3–4) |
| Extra terms | Adds a pretraining log-likelihood term $\gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\log\pi(x)]$ (p. 9) | None. Eq. 3 is pure reward plus KL (p. 3) |
| Reward model | Separate trained RM $r_\theta$. The value function is initialised from it (p. 9) | No explicit RM. The implicit reward is $\hat r_\theta=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{ref}}}$, so the policy itself acts as the reward model (pp. 4–5) |
| Optimiser | PPO on fresh samples from the policy (p. 9) | One binary cross-entropy loss on a fixed preference dataset, with no RL loop (pp. 2, 4–5) |
| Role of $\beta$ | Weight on the per-token KL penalty (p. 9) | Sets the KL strength and also scales the logits in the loss. Each example's gradient is weighted by how badly the implicit reward misorders the pair (p. 5) |

DPO says it optimises the same objective as PPO-based RLHF, and does so more efficiently. On their sentiment task, its reward/KL trade-off "strictly dominates PPO" (pp. 8–9). Even so, InstructGPT's actual objective is not exactly DPO's Eq. 3, because of the $\gamma$ pretraining term. Only the plain "PPO" variant with $\gamma = 0$ matches it.

One thing to watch when comparing the papers: they swap the subscripts. InstructGPT writes the reward as $r_\theta$ and the policy as $\pi_\phi$ (p. 9). DPO writes the reward as $r_\phi$ and the policy as $\pi_\theta$ (p. 3).

The page numbers are the PDF pages. For the parts I checked (pp. 3–5 and 9), they match the numbers printed on the pages.
